title: Who is Timor-Leste's dancing prime minister Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão?
summary: Xanana Gusmão's dancing drew cheers at ASEAN, but his political career stretches back to Timor-Leste's decades-long struggle for independence.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 1:08pm

MANILA, Philippines — He danced with Filipino performers to the beat of P-pop group SB19, drew cheers from fellow Southeast Asian leaders and became one of the crowd favorites at the closing ceremony of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila.
The man was Timor-Leste Prime Minister Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão, who joined performers dancing to SB19's rendition of "Together in Motion," the official theme song of the 2026 ASEAN Summit.
But it was not the first time he danced during his visit. He also joined in when Filipino young artists welcomed him upon his arrival and showed off a few moves during the summit's opening night.

But Gusmão is known for more than his dancing. Before becoming prime minister, he led the armed resistance against Indonesia's occupation of East Timor, spent years in prison and later became the country's first president after independence.
From journalist to resistance leader
Born on June 20, 1946, in Manatuto, Gusmão grew up when Timor-Leste was still under Portuguese rule, according to the Timor-Leste government's official biography.
He worked in public administration before joining the Portuguese military. He later became a journalist and photographer for the newspaper A Voz de Timor.

His involvement in the independence movement began in 1974, when he joined the Timorese Social Democratic Association, which later became the Revolutionary Front for an Independent East Timor, or FRETILIN.

Indonesia invaded East Timor on Dec. 7, 1975, shortly after the territory declared independence from Portugal. The occupation led to years of armed resistance and a long struggle for self-determination.
Gusmão became one of the leading figures in that resistance. After the death of FRETILIN leader Nicolau Lobato in 1978, he helped reorganize the movement.
In 1981, he was elected leader of the resistance and commander-in-chief of its armed wing, the Armed Forces for the National Liberation of East Timor, or FALINTIL.
He also worked to unite different groups seeking independence. In 1988, he helped establish the National Council of Maubere Resistance, which later became the National Council of Timorese Resistance.
Imprisonment and independence
According to the Timor-Leste government's official biography, Indonesian forces captured Gusmão on Nov. 20, 1992, and sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

His arrest did not end his involvement in the independence movement. He continued to communicate with resistance leaders while in detention and used his time in prison to study Indonesian, English and law. He also wrote poetry and painted.
He was transferred to house arrest in February 1999 and released on September 7 that year.

Months earlier, on Aug. 30, 1999, East Timorese voted in a United Nations-backed referendum on whether to accept an autonomy proposal within Indonesia. A majority rejected the proposal, paving the way for the end of Indonesian rule.
Timor-Leste became an independent country on May 20, 2002, and Gusmão was elected its first president.
He served until 2007, when he became prime minister. He returned to the post in 2012 but resigned in 2015, saying he wanted to give younger leaders an opportunity to take over.

Gusmão remained involved in government, later serving as minister of planning and strategic investment. He also led negotiations with Australia over maritime boundaries, which resulted in a treaty ratified in 2019.
He returned as prime minister on July 1, 2023, after his party, the National Congress for Timorese Reconstruction, won the parliamentary elections.
Timor-Leste's decades-long bid to join ASEAN
Timor-Leste's push to join ASEAN began decades before it became the bloc's 11th member.

President José Ramos-Horta has been among the country's strongest advocates for regional integration. He discussed the idea with then-Indonesian Foreign Minister Adam Malik as early as 1974, when Timor-Leste was still under Portuguese rule.

Ramos-Horta, who served as president from 2007 to 2012 and returned to the post in 2022, also helped advance the country's bid for membership. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996 for his work toward a peaceful resolution of the conflict in East Timor.
Timor-Leste formally applied for ASEAN membership on March 4, 2011, during Ramos-Horta's presidency, with Gusmão then serving as prime minister.
The application, however, did not lead to immediate membership. ASEAN had to assess whether the young country had the resources, personnel and institutions needed to meet the bloc's commitments.

In November 2022, ASEAN leaders agreed in principle to admit Timor-Leste and granted it observer status. They later approved a roadmap in May 2023 to help the country meet the requirements for full membership.
Under Gusmão's government, Timor-Leste worked to comply with the requirements across ASEAN's political-security, economic and socio-cultural pillars.
Philippines backs membership bid
The Philippines has supported Timor-Leste's bid to join ASEAN since 2002, with successive administrations maintaining the country's position.
Former president Benigno Aquino III also pledged support for Timor-Leste's membership in 2013.
In May 2023, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. assured then-Timor-Leste Prime Minister Taur Matan Ruak of Manila's support during a meeting on the sidelines of the 42nd ASEAN Summit in Indonesia.
"In the Philippines, you have a partner. We have always been supportive," Marcos said.

Marcos reiterated this during Timorese President José Ramos-Horta's state visit to the Philippines in November 2023. Ramos-Horta said the two countries shared a "long history of solidarity and support for each other."
The Philippines maintained its support even after a diplomatic disagreement with Timor-Leste over the extradition of former Negros Oriental congressman Arnolfo Teves Jr.

In March 2025, a Timorese court rejected the Philippines' request to extradite Teves, who faces multiple murder charges, including over the killing of former governor Roel Degamo. The Philippine government criticized the ruling, saying it went against the trust and cooperation expected among ASEAN members.
In May 2025, the Philippines again expressed support for Timor-Leste's membership ahead of the 46th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur.

Then Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Theresa Lazaro said Manila had committed to supporting Timor-Leste's accession and helping implement the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 following a preparatory meeting on May 24.
The Philippines' renewed assurance came just two months after the disagreement over Teves.
Timor-Leste becomes ASEAN's 11th member

ASEAN leaders agreed to admit Timor-Leste during the bloc's 47th summit in May 2025. The country formally became the 11th member on Oct. 26, 2025, during the 47th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
Gusmão signed the declaration on Timor-Leste's admission, while Ramos-Horta attended the ceremony.
Timor-Leste was the first country to join ASEAN since Cambodia in 1999. Its entry also meant the ASEAN emblem, which features rice stalks representing its member states, would have an 11th stalk.
The Manila summit in November 2026 was Timor-Leste's first full ASEAN summit as a member of the regional bloc. — with reports from Cristina Chi, Ian Laqui, Helen Flores and Agence France-Presse
